name: Agriculture
blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

points.desc: Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray, autonomous tractors) is the reference commercial deployment.
points.name: Precision ag is shipping product

points.desc: Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its fortnightly AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms - variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, autonomous equipment. The federal measurement layer.
points.name: USDA ERS measures US adoption

points.desc: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact.
points.name: FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally

points.desc: The AgriFoodTech investment research tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software - the sector's funding barometer.
points.name: AgFunder indexes the investment flow

points.desc: Planet Labs' high-resolution imagery, Descartes Labs' geospatial ML, and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators supply the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection.
points.name: The satellite layer feeds the models

points.desc: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production.
points.name: AEM tracks the machinery standards

points.desc: The nonprofit consortium sets the open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites - the plumbing under everything else.
points.name: AgGateway makes the data interoperable

points.desc: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.
points.name: ISPA bridges the science and the field

points.desc: The 100 Million Farmers initiative tracks AI adoption through the lens of climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.
points.name: WEF tracks climate-smart adoption

points.desc: Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are the large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning.
points.name: The agribusiness platforms run the prescriptions

points.desc: CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application - the equipment layer beyond Deere.
points.name: CNH and Raven automate the other fleets

points.desc: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide; Monarch builds electric driverless tractors - narrow AI shipping as farm equipment.
points.name: The pure-plays attack single problems

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey recorded 13.7% of agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting firms reporting AI use in the prior period, with the most recent figure suppressed, leaving measured adoption modest and incomplete at the national level. The USDA Economic Research Service publishes the longer-running data series on precision-agriculture uptake across US farms, covering variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, and autonomous equipment, and represents the primary federal measurement layer for the sector. The International Society of Precision Agriculture connects academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice, while AgGateway, a global nonprofit, sets the open data standards that allow AI models to ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites, providing the interoperability layer beneath most deployments.

What AI is actually doing on farms spans several distinct functions. Climate FieldView, Bayer's digital farming platform, turns soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions using machine learning, and farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of plus 5 bushels per acre compared to users who wrote their own scripts, the clearest ROI figure available from the sourced material. Carbon Robotics deploys what it calls physical AI through its LaserWeeder, a machine that identifies and kills weeds with computer vision and lasers rather than herbicide, trained on what the company describes as the world's largest and most diverse agricultural dataset collected by its machines in the field. Planet Labs supplies the satellite observation layer, providing daily high-resolution Earth imagery and derived analytics that feed crop-stress detection and yield prediction models used across the sector.

Investment flows give a rough sense of where the industry is heading commercially. Per AgFunder, which tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software, global agrifoodtech funding reached 16 billion dollars in 2024, a 4% drop from 2023, before recovering to 16.2 billion dollars in 2025, nearly flat year over year at negative 3%. AgFunder notes investors are writing checks more selectively, directing capital toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue, a signal that early-stage enthusiasm is giving way to demand for demonstrated results. Developing markets showed stronger momentum, with agrifoodtech funding in those regions growing 63% between 2023 and 2024, compared to a 4% decline globally, and Asia-Pacific agrifoodtech startups raised 4.2 billion dollars through October 2024, a 38% increase over the same period in 2023.

The FAO's digital agriculture program is working to extend these tools into lower-income contexts, including through the Innovate Africa Challenge, launched in partnership with Smart Africa, which aims to accelerate AI solutions addressing agricultural and climate pressures on the continent. African agrifoodtech funding remains a small fraction of global investment, at just 1.6% per AgFunder, and while it showed mild recovery in the first half of 2024 with 145 million dollars raised, a 1.6% year-over-year increase, it follows a challenging 2023 in which investment declined 62% to 275 million dollars. The gap between where AI agriculture tools are being built and where smallholder food production is concentrated remains a structural constraint on global uptake.

For a decision-maker considering deployment, the sourced material points to a sector where proven ROI exists in specific, narrow applications, particularly input optimization through platforms like FieldView and mechanical weed control through vision-guided robotics, but where broader adoption is constrained by data interoperability, the standards work AgGateway is still completing, and the capital selectivity AgFunder documents. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers is actively shaping policy and standards around autonomous machinery, and the machinery standardization environment is still forming. Anyone deploying should expect to engage with data standards questions early, treat vendor ROI claims as context-dependent rather than universal, and recognize that the investment environment, while recovering, is rewarding demonstrated unit economics over promise.
